title: Covid Variant PJ.2.1 Is Spreading Abroad: What Indians Need to Know
excerpt: PJ.2.1 rose to 25.2% of sequenced samples in Ontario, but there is no evidence it causes more severe illness and no confirmed detection in India in the reports so far.
body:
• PJ.2.1, a heavily mutated SARS-CoV-2 lineage first sampled in Ontario, Canada, on May 2, 2026, has since been detected in the United States, Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, Israel, France and Spain.
  • In Ontario it rose from 1.1% of sequenced samples in late June to late July to 25.2% of sequenced samples from September 20 to October 17 - that is a share of samples sent for sequencing, not a share of all infections in the population.
  • There is currently no evidence PJ.2.1 causes more severe illness, more hospitalisations or more deaths than other circulating variants, and the WHO has not designated it a variant of concern, interest or under monitoring in the lists cited by these reports.
  • What this means for you: there is no confirmed detection of PJ.2.1 in India in these reports. If you develop fever, cough or a sore throat, test if the result would change treatment, stay away from older or immunocompromised family members, and seek urgent care for difficulty breathing - the WHO COVID-19 fact sheet lists the warning signs.

A new Covid lineage, PJ.2.1, is drawing attention because of how fast its share of sequenced samples rose in Ontario - not because doctors have found it makes people sicker. Reports in Jagran Josh and the Daily Jagran, drawing on research published in the Journal of Infection in October 2026, describe PJ.2.1 as a saltation variant: a lineage that appeared with an unusually large number of genetic changes at once, rather than accumulating them slowly.

Where it came from and where it has been found

PJ.2.1 evolved from MC.10.1.7, a descendant of the JN.1 lineage, according to the Daily Jagran. The earliest documented sample was collected in Ontario on May 2, 2026. It was later recorded in New York City on June 30, 2026, and has since been detected in other parts of Canada and the United States and in Singapore, Australia, New Zealand, Israel, France and Spain.

The Ontario numbers are the ones driving headlines. Jagran Josh reports PJ.2.1 accounted for 1.1% of sequenced coronavirus samples from June 28 to July 25, 16.9% from August 23 to September 19, and 25.2% from September 20 to October 17. Those percentages describe only the samples laboratories sequenced. They do not mean one in four people in Ontario was infected with PJ.2.1, and coverage cautions that gaps in sequencing can distort the picture.

What the laboratory work does - and does not - show

Laboratory research found changes in the spike protein and stronger binding to the ACE2 receptor, the doorway the virus uses to enter human cells. That is a laboratory finding. It does not by itself prove the variant spreads faster between people in homes, offices or aircraft, and it says nothing about severity.

On immunity, researchers did not find substantially greater evasion of vaccine-induced antibodies than for most other variants tested. Serum from people who received an LP.8.1-adapted vaccine neutralised PJ.2.1, though neutralisation was about 1.8-fold lower than for the LP.8.1 reference. That is also laboratory evidence; real-world protection against infection or hospitalisation has not been established for this lineage.

Symptoms and absolute risk

No symptom is unique to PJ.2.1. The WHO lists fever, chills and sore throat as the most common symptoms for currently circulating variants, with cough, runny or blocked nose, headache, muscle aches, fatigue, breathlessness and changes in taste or smell also reported. Because those symptoms overlap with influenza and the common cold, the WHO stresses that symptoms alone cannot identify which virus caused an illness - testing is needed when the answer affects treatment.

On the question readers ask first - is it more dangerous? - the current answer from these sources is no, not on the evidence available. Jagran Josh states there is insufficient clinical evidence that PJ.2.1 causes more hospitalisations, more severe disease or more deaths. In absolute terms, the sources report no PJ.2.1-specific hospitalisation or death rate at all, so no honest percentage-point risk can be calculated for an individual reader. The people who remain at higher risk of severe Covid in general are older adults, immunocompromised people and people with chronic conditions such as diabetes, heart or lung disease, according to the WHO.

What Indians should do now

For India, Jagran Josh notes genomic surveillance runs through INSACOG, but the reports do not confirm detection of PJ.2.1 in the country. There is no basis in these sources for lockdowns, travel bans or panic buying, and none is recommended in them.

The practical steps are the familiar ones, and they matter most inside multigenerational homes common in Indian and diaspora families: stay home and away from others while you have Covid-like symptoms, test when a result would change treatment or protect a vulnerable relative, improve indoor ventilation, and talk to your doctor about staying up to date on Covid vaccination if you are older or at high risk. Seek medical care promptly for difficulty breathing at rest, confusion, persistent chest pain or pressure, or inability to speak in full sentences - the severe symptoms listed by the WHO.
